title: Sequence containers and invalidation
summary: Choose an owning sequence and keep references valid across its modifications.
objectives: Distinguish a vector’s size from its capacity.
Predict which operations can invalidate borrowed access.
Choose between fixed and growing sequences by their required operations.

parts.title: Choose a sequence by its behavior

blocks.text: A container owns a collection of elements and defines how they are arranged and accessed. std::vector is a useful starting point for a sequence whose length can change. It stores ordinary elements contiguously and manages their storage automatically. std::array represents a fixed number of elements as part of its own value. Neither choice requires writing new or delete, so the first design question can focus on the application’s required operations.

A vector’s size is the number of existing elements. Its capacity is the number of elements that can fit in its current allocation without reallocation. reserve requests enough capacity for a future number of elements but does not increase size. resize changes the number of existing elements. Confusing these operations can lead to indexing storage where no vector element exists, even when memory has already been reserved.

blocks.caption: Complete C++20 program — main.cpp

blocks.text: The example reserves space for at least four elements and then appends two strings. It deliberately prints a comparison about capacity rather than its exact value, because the implementation may allocate more space than requested. The two strings are the only accessible elements at that point. After erasing the first element, the second becomes the first, and the vector’s size is one.

No element reference or iterator is retained across the erasure. That matters because vector erasure invalidates iterators and references at or after the erased position. Reallocation during insertion is broader: it invalidates access to every element and the old end iterator. A vector object can stay alive throughout these operations while its borrowed element access becomes invalid. Reacquiring access afterward makes the example’s ownership reasoning straightforward.

Choose another sequence container when its operation guarantees solve an actual requirement. A deque supports growth at both ends; list and forward_list have node-based relationships and different iterator guarantees. These differences do not make one container universally faster. Traversal locality, allocation overhead, element size, and the actual operation mix matter. Detailed implementations and data-structure proofs belong in a separate algorithms course.

Check bounds before unchecked indexing, or use at when a checked access with an exception on failure matches the interface. front requires a nonempty sequence. In this program the preceding insertions and single erasure establish that precondition. A general-purpose function receiving an arbitrary vector must establish it explicitly. The library provides useful contracts, but the caller must connect those contracts to the particular program state.

blocks.prompt: After reserve(4) on an empty vector, may the program assign to titles[0]?
blocks.explanation: No. reserve changes available capacity but creates no elements. The vector is still empty. push_back, emplace_back, or an appropriate resize must create an element before indexing it.
